full_judgment:
2. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs appellants has taken me through the judgment of the Courts below and other relevant materials. The learned Advocate submits that he would press only one ground in attacking the impugned order of Settlement made by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Chittagong and that ground would be the ground of mala fide. The learned Advocate submits that the Courts below have not considered the point that the Settlement made by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) was void and illegal because of malafide and as such their judgments suffer from illegality. The Malafide canvassed by the learned Advocate is that the settlement was made without making the necessary inquiry as required by Rule 54 of the Government Estate Manual read: with section 77 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy. Act. The learned Advocate submits that the failure to make such enquiry was malafide in law and vitiated the settlement. 

 Rule 54 of the Government Estate Manual reads as 

 "54 Equitable distribution of land amongst the bonafide cultivators is one of the main purposes for acquisition of all rent-receiving interest. The chief restrictions on settlement of land imposed by section 76 of the State Acquisition Act are e. (I) settlement should-not be made with anyone who is not a bonafide cultivator; (2) settlement should not be made with any person unless he is a person to whom transfer of land can be made under section 90 of the said Act. The foregoing provisions of the Act will be enforced vigorously. Except under the special orders of the Board of Revenue, the Collectors and Re-venue Deputy Collectors empowered to make settlement of land should not settle agricultural lands with non-cultivators or with persons who have already more than five acres of cultivable lands. If In any case, limit of transfer prescribed by Section 90 of the act is proposed to be exceeded under the provision to that section, sanction of the Board should be sought for." 

 Section 76 of the State Acquisition and Truancy Act reads as follows:- 

 3. Neither Rule 54 of the Estates Manual nor section 76 of the S.A. & T. Act provides for any enquiry. No rule made under the S.A. & T. Act and having a statutory force providing for any such enquiry could be placed before me the rules of the Estates Manual are in the nature of department instructions and cannot be said to have any force of law. Mr. A K.M. Shafiqur Rahman learned Advocate, however, submits that in order to achieve the objectives of the scheme of settlement envisaged in sub-section (1) of section 76 of S.A. and T. Act, and enquiry is necessary sub-section (1) of  this section provides that lands vesting in the Government shall be absolutely at the disposal of the Government and that Government shall be competent to Make settlement of such land in accordance with such  rule as it may makes in this behalf. It is evident that the lands vesting in the Government under the State. Acquisition and Tenancy Act and held in khas by the Government are absolutely at the disposal of the Government and the Government is competent to make settlement of such lands in accordance with rules. Even though no rules under statute appear to have been framed, it cannot be argued that Government is powerless in the matter of settlement of land. The first proviso to sub-section (i) prohibits settlement a. person to whom transfer is prohibited under section 90. The second proviso to that section lays down a rule of preference in the matter of settlement. Some sort of enquiry appears to be necessary for attaining the objective of section 76. But omission or failure to make such enquiry does not appear either to constitute an illegality or even a material irregularity which would vitiate the settlement Sub-section (2) of section 76 clearly provides that no Civil Court shall entertain any application or suit concerning any matter relating to the settlement by any, officer of the Government Of any land under sub-section (1). In view of the bar imposed by sub-section (2), any settlement made under subsection (1) could not be questioned before the Civil Court. It may be stated here that the competency of the Additional Deputy Commissioner to make the impugned settlement was not questioned as being without jurisdiction. I am unable to accept the view of Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman that the failure to make any enquiry or to cause an enquiry to be made by the Additional Deputy Commissioner is malafide in law. The learned Advocate could not place any authority to support his view. In the case before me, on fact, there is also no allegation that the defendants with whom the settlement has been made are not bonafide cultivators or that the defendants are or any of them is a person to whom transfer of land could not be made under section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The failure of the authorities of the Government to make any enquiry has not therefore resulted in frustrating the object of section 76 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Such a failure cannot obviously lead to any legal consequence and can, by no means, constitute malafide either in law or in fact. There is no substance in this Appeal.
